articles.title: Saved for Sunday: What to see when you can’t see You Can See Everything
articles.summary: One of the biggest films of the year has just come out in North America, but Australians will have to wait a month. Today, Sian Cain talks us through the You Can See Everything buzz.
body: The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’
Leading questions: A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable?

What to watch | Australian author Diana Reid’s Austenian leanings have been apparent ever since she titled her first novel Love and Virtue. Now she has turned her hand to a full period piece, writing the script for Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility adaptation starring Daisy Edgar-Jones. With the film in cinemas now, we spoke to Reid about the sisterly love at the centre of the story and learning to speak in Regency English.

What to read | Australian journalist Richard Cooke has turned his considerable research skills and incisive tone towards a subject so big, he says “writing an ‘exhaustive’ book on it is impossible”: Wikipedia. His new book The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia looks at the people behind the sprawling encyclopedia and finds a committed and wholesome (if sometimes fractious) community of ingenious weirdos.

articles.title: The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’
articles.summary: Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship. Find more stories from the moment I knew series. Anne and I met in Melbourne in 1997 when we were cast in a production of Hamlet.
body: At first it was a little awkward, but humour was the key. We’d sit on the dusty rehearsal room floor in our tracksuits while the director was working with another actor. Instead of practising our lines, we’d flip through the faded 70s magazines left in the corner and make jokes about what the models in flares or with chopped beards might be saying as they shot the images.

One day by chance I flipped to the horoscopes. I asked Anne what the stars could have in store for us in 1972. She told me her sign was Scorpio – the same as mine. My aim was just to laugh at the bullshit of horoscopes but when I read it out, it stopped me cold: “You have met someone now through work who will be one of the most important people in your life, perhaps a partner and soulmate.”

It was weird and uncanny but we just laughed it off. I felt embarrassed because it sounded like some kind of calculated romantic ploy. I quickly flicked to the next page but somewhere in my brain I knew it was the truth.
points: Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship.

articles.title: ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone
articles.summary: Athletes’ scramble to control – and monetise – their digital identities at the cutting edge of AI rights deals. Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast.
body: The Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world.

This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness.

Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit.

This video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transform the future of image rights and sports content.

articles.title: Inside the Couture Council Luncheon, Where Diane von Furstenberg Was Celebrated as a “Force of Nature”
articles.summary: The 2026 Couture Council Award was presented to designer, author, and philanthropist, Diane von Furstenberg at Gotham Hall in New York. Fashion industry veterans, emerging designers, and supporters alike showed up wearing signature DVF prints.
body: “All my life, I wanted to be the woman in charge—and then I became a woman in charge of a little dress,” Diane von Furstenberg told an audience at Gotham Hall as she accepted the 2026 Couture Council Award. Of course, those familiar with the designer’s story knew she was referencing the title of her 2024 documentary, Woman in Charge, which chronicles her illustrious life and journey to building a global fashion empire.

More than 50 years after she created her groundbreaking wrap dress, the design still resonates, as evidenced by the room full of people dressed in the silhouette on Thursday at FIT/The Museum at FIT’s annual Couture Council luncheon. Martha Stewart, Narciso Rodriguez, Nicole Miller, Linda Fargo, Fern Mallis, Erin Walsh, and Candace Bushnell were among those who turned out in style to celebrate an industry icon.

articles.title: Lauren Santo Domingo Brought a Stylish Crowd to Colombia to Fete the Four Seasons Cartagena
articles.summary: Colombian culture and fashion took center stage at a weekend-long celebration for the newly opened Four Seasons Cartagena.
body: Summer wardrobes may be packed away until next year, but this past weekend, a fashionable group traded crisp air and trench coats for tropics-friendly resortwear at the Four Seasons Cartagena. Guests—including Lauren and Andrés Santo Domingo; Alejandro and Charlotte Santo Domingo; Andrea and Tatiana Casiraghi; chef Mario Carbone and Cait Bailey Carbone; artist Olympia Scarry; designers Johanna Ortiz, Danielle Frankel Hirsch, Conner Ives, and Annie Doble; and entrepreneur Jen Rubio—took over the sprawling property’s 131 rooms for a multi-day celebration of Colombian culture.

“The city has a sense of magical realism,” remarked Lauren Santo Domingo, citing Cartagena’s prodigal son, Gabriel García Márquez. “The first time I came here, I really felt like I was transported and I was somewhere different, unlike anywhere I’ve ever been: every corner on every street, every balcony, is covered in bougainvillea.”

articles.title: How To Achieve the Soft, Plump Look of “Mochi Skin”
articles.summary: The "mochi skin" trend takes its name from the traditional Japanese rice cake treat famous for its bouncy texture, plump appearance, and smooth surface.
body: Beauty trends are constantly evolving, and this year clearly favors a more textured and luminous complexion—one that isn’t excessively shiny. On red carpets and social media alike, celebs and trendsetters seem to be moving away from ultra-glowy, glazed donut finishes in favor of skin that retains its texture, depth, and natural glow.

In other words, move over glass skin —right now, it’s all about “mochi skin.” This latest obsession from Japan focuses on a plump, fresh finish, one that calls to mind the softness and suppleness of the famous Japanese dessert for which it is named.

As mentioned, this new skin trend takes its name from mochi, a traditional Japanese rice cake treat famous for its bouncy texture, plump appearance, and smooth, slightly translucent surface. It’s easy to see how those descriptors would translate into an appealing skin look—after all, who among us doesn’t want “plump” “bouncy” and “smooth” skin? When it comes to mochi skin, the idea is to create an almost indulgent-looking complexion—one that appears as soft, smooth, and delicately plump as a delicious mochi treat.
points: The "mochi skin" trend takes its name from the traditional Japanese rice cake treat famous for its bouncy texture, plump appearance, and smooth surface.

articles.title: This Joan Crawford Classic Still Has Something to Teach Us About Women—and the Clothes They Wear
articles.summary: The 1939 hit The Women spawned fashion trends, resurrected careers, launched new ones, and has fallen in and out of favor. Now, it’s enjoying another reconsideration, thanks to a new book by actress-turned-film scholar Illeana Douglas.
body: Growing up, Illeana Douglas spent a lot of time with her Oscar-winning grandfather in his Upper West Side apartment, where, salon-style, he would regularly host writers like Gore Vidal and screen legends like Myrna Loy. That duality seemed to inform the adult Illeana’s interests. In her twenties, she performed in a sketch comedy group at night, while holding down a day job as a film publicist, working on campaigns for future classics like The Princess Bride, The Untouchables, and Moonstruck.

She entered the ‘90s as one of Hollywood’s most reliable character actresses, stealing scenes in zeitgeist-defining films like Goodfellas and To Die For. “I would always get the part where I'd look through the script, and I’d go, ‘I don’t see any lines here,’” she says. “And they’d say, ‘Well, you'll come up with something brilliant’... So it was writing—but not realizing I was writing.”
